criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban domestic water supply service access in Blantyre, Malawi, including household bill affordability, service disconnections, reconnection barriers, and differential coverage between low-income areas (49%) and formal medium/high-income areas (96%) alongside utility performance benchmarking.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines public water utility governance, statutory commercialization mandates (Water Works Act of 1995), tariff policy, and revenue-collection administration. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, although a substantial part of the paper benchmarks general utility efficiency (working ratio, unaccounted-for water, staff per 1000 connections), Sections 3, 4.1.2, and 4.1.3 directly examine rule-type mechanisms governing household water access: rising-block tariff and cost-recovery rules (including government regulatory rejection of the proposed 2009 tariff increase and uniform residential volumetric tariffs), administrative payment-updating delays in bank bill-payment arrangements causing wrongful disconnections, disconnection enforcement for non-payment, and a MK1000 (US$7.09) reconnection fee deterring reconnection.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical mixed-methods case study combining review of national legal/policy documents and Blantyre Water Board operational/financial records (2001-2009), interviews with three utility officials, and interviews with a random sample of 100 low-income domestic customers across three areas.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports access-relevant outcomes at the household level, specifically affordability (house connection bills accounting for 4.4% of household income in low-income areas, deemed high by 70% of interviewed customers; average domestic bill of MK1125 or US$8/month) and exclusion/disconnection (8 of 100 interviewed customers disconnected despite having already paid via bank; increasing numbers of disconnected customers failing to reconnect; 17 of 100 citing the MK1000 reconnection fee as exorbitant), alongside contextual data on service coverage and supply continuity.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies both units of analysis clearly: Blantyre Water Board (public parastatal water utility) and 100 randomly selected domestic customer households in three low-income areas of Blantyre (Chilobwe, Misesa, and Nancholi), with identifiable tariff/billing/disconnection exposures, affordability/disconnection outcomes, and empirical case-study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: A total of 100 domestic customers were selected at random from the low-income areas of Chilobwe (30 customers), Misesa (40 customers) and Nancholi (30 customers) for interview in order to get an overview of the customer perspective of what was documented.

The utility applies the rising block tariff (see Tables 4 and 5) with the aim of the rich subsidizing the service to the poor. Customers were being charged based on the 2008 tariffs because implementation of tariffs proposed for 2009 was rejected by the government on the basis that the utility would be transferring the cost of its inefﬁciency to the customers.
From those interviewed, some eight paid up customers indicated that they had at some point been disconnected having already paid through the bank.

Based on the tariff structure (see Section 4.1.3) in the low-income areas the bills for house connections account for 4.4% of household income, a ﬁgure deemed to be on the higher side by the utility and some 70% of the customers interviewed.

The number of disconnected customers has increased with time resulting in increased bad debtors as often customers do not pay for reconnection. Some 17 customers out of the 100 interviewed cited the reconnection fee of MK1000 (US$7.09) as exorbitant.

raw_response.exposure: Public utility tariff and cost-recovery rules (rising block tariff structure, uniform residential volumetric charges, government rejection of proposed 2009 tariff increase, MK1000 reconnection fee) and billing/payment administration and disconnection enforcement (including delayed bank-payment account reconciliation) under the Water Works Act of 1995 mandate.
raw_response.outcome: Household water bill affordability (4.4% of household income in low-income areas; perceived high burden among 70% of interviewed customers) and service disconnection/non-reconnection (wrongful disconnection of 8/100 paid-up bank payers; rising disconnections and non-reconnection linked to the MK1000 reconnection fee cited as exorbitant by 17/100 customers), alongside utility-level financial/operational performance indicators.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Blantyre Water Board (parastatal urban water utility serving Blantyre City, Malawi; 3 officials interviewed: Internal Audit Manager, 1 Zone Manager, 1 Projects and Planning Engineer) and 100 randomly selected domestic customer households in three low-income areas of Blantyre: Chilobwe (n=30), Misesa (n=40), and Nancholi (n=30).
raw_response.rationale: Although framed primarily around benchmarking public water utility performance (working ratio, bill collection efficiency, unaccounted-for water, and staffing per 1000 connections), this empirical case study also collects primary interview data from 100 randomly sampled low-income domestic customers in Blantyre, Malawi, alongside utility documentation and staff interviews. It directly examines rule-type tariff, administrative billing/reconciliation, and disconnection/reconnection fee mechanisms governing household water affordability (bills consuming 4.4% of household income) and service exclusion/disconnection (wrongful disconnections from delayed bank account updates and persistent non-reconnection due to the MK1000 reconnection fee). It therefore meets all systematic-review inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (noting that Criterion 6 quantitative effect-size extractability is a meta-analysis gate rather than a review-inclusion gate).
raw_response.study_design: Empirical mixed-methods case study (documentary review of legal/policy and utility records, key-informant interviews with 3 utility officials, and random-sample interviews of 100 low-income domestic customers)
